Trying to Conceive

Ovulation after miscarriage: when it returns and trying again

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Fertility can return before the first period after a miscarriage. That does not mean you have to be ready for another pregnancy at the same time. Recovery, completion of any treatment, your previous fertility history and how you feel all belong in the conversation about what comes next.

Ovulation can return before your first period

After an early miscarriage, ovulation can happen as soon as about two weeks later. This is an earliest possibility, not a dependable appointment in your calendar. The timing varies with the pregnancy, recovery and how quickly pregnancy hormones fall. You can conceive before seeing another period, so use contraception if you do not want a new pregnancy yet.

Bleeding after a loss is part of the recovery process and is not necessarily a new menstrual period. Record the miscarriage and bleeding separately in a tracking app rather than assuming that its first day starts an ordinary cycle with ovulation on day 14. Calendar predictions are particularly uncertain during this transition.

Bleeding and periods settle at different speeds

Bleeding often lasts around one to two weeks after an early loss, and it can last longer depending on how the miscarriage is managed. A later loss may have a different recovery pattern. Follow your own discharge advice; several weeks of ongoing bleeding should not simply be dismissed as normal spotting.

For someone whose cycles were regular, the next period commonly arrives in about four to six weeks, although it can take up to eight weeks. Cycles may take a few months to become predictable. If they were irregular before pregnancy, they may remain irregular afterward. Check with your care team if the expected recovery or return of periods is not happening, especially if a pregnancy test remains positive.

Do you need to wait six months before trying again?

There is no single waiting interval that suits every loss. Older advice recommended six months, partly because of concerns about maternal anemia, premature birth and low birthweight. That advice drew on evidence with important limitations, including research that did not reliably separate miscarriage from induced abortion. It should not be turned into a universal rule for an uncomplicated early miscarriage.

A 2017 systematic review found that intervals shorter than six months were associated with fewer repeat miscarriages and preterm births, while pooled results did not show a clear increase in stillbirth, low birthweight or pre-eclampsia. A Scottish study also found favorable outcomes, including live births, among people who conceived sooner. These associations do not prove that trying immediately prevents complications.

More recent Norwegian birth-registry research did not find higher rates of the studied pregnancy complications when conception followed miscarriage by less than three months. An NIH study also found no evidence that everyone needs a three-month delay after an uncomplicated early loss. Neither result is a reason to rush: the studies cannot settle every personal medical circumstance or explain every possible outcome.

Make the timing decision around your recovery

A useful starting point is to finish the recommended follow-up and ask whether any reason to delay applies to you. Bleeding and other miscarriage symptoms should have settled before resuming sex. Waiting for one normal period may make a later pregnancy easier to date, but it is not a universal requirement for a healthy next pregnancy after an uncomplicated early loss.

Significant blood loss or anemia, infection, a later miscarriage, or treatment for an ectopic or molar pregnancy can require a different plan. Do not apply general early-miscarriage advice to those situations. Ask the clinician who managed your care when pregnancy testing, follow-up or treatment needs to be complete, and when trying again is appropriate.

What fertility signs can tell you

As ovulation approaches, cervical mucus may become clearer, more slippery and stretchy. Some people feel mild discomfort on one side, while others notice no pain at all. Neither symptom proves that an egg has been released. Strong, persistent or worsening pain after a loss should be assessed, not labeled an ovulation sign.

Ovulation predictor tests detect a rise in luteinizing hormone, or LH, which usually precedes egg release. They can help identify a likely fertile time, but a positive test does not guarantee ovulation or pregnancy. Recent pregnancy can make some tests misleading; follow the instructions for the exact product and ask your care team how to interpret testing while pregnancy hormones are still clearing.

The fertile window generally includes the five days before ovulation and the day of ovulation itself. It is not limited to a single day or to the day a test changes. Tracking is optional: it should help you make sense of a cycle, not create another task you must get perfect.

How to use basal temperature without overreading it

If you choose temperature tracking, use the same appropriate thermometer and measurement method each day. Take the reading on waking, before getting out of bed, at a similar time, and record it. A small sustained rise may suggest that ovulation has already occurred.

Temperature is therefore better at showing a pattern afterward than predicting the exact moment to try. The most fertile days are usually before the rise. There is no single temperature increase that works for everyone, and illness, disrupted sleep or medication can blur the pattern. Do not use temperature alone to diagnose a fertility problem or to assume pregnancy is impossible.

When to ask for fertility help

Many people go on to have a successful pregnancy after miscarriage, but no percentage can promise when you will conceive. In general, seek a fertility assessment after 12 months of trying if you are under 35, or after six months if you are 35 or older. Over 40, discussing an assessment sooner is appropriate.

Do not restart the clock without considering your earlier history. If conception was already difficult, cycles are very irregular, or you have a known condition affecting fertility, ask for advice earlier. An assessment can consider ovulation and other relevant factors, including a partner’s fertility where applicable; it is not limited to deciding which day to have sex.

Symptoms that need attention during recovery

Get urgent medical help for very heavy bleeding, severe or increasing abdominal pain, faintness or feeling seriously unwell. Shoulder-tip pain with pregnancy-related bleeding or pain can also be an emergency. Do not wait until a particular number of pads has been used if you feel weak or dizzy.

Fever, chills, an unpleasant-smelling discharge or bleeding that persists or gets heavier need prompt advice from the service managing the miscarriage. Follow the pregnancy-test and review schedule they provide. Ongoing symptoms can need assessment for infection or remaining pregnancy tissue rather than more home ovulation testing.

A previous loss does not predict the next pregnancy by itself

Many early miscarriages are one-off events related to the pregnancy’s chromosomes. Age and pregnancy history influence future risk, but fixed percentages after one, two or three losses cannot accurately describe every person. A longer time to conceive is a reason to review fertility, not proof that a future pregnancy will miscarry.

Repeated losses deserve an individualized discussion. Some services begin investigation after two miscarriages; others use three, or investigate earlier when the history suggests a problem. Depending on the circumstances, assessment may include genetic, uterine, hormonal or immune-related causes. Testing is not simply a genetic screen, and sometimes no definite cause is found.

Health preparation should support you, not assign blame

Miscarriage risk rises with age, especially after 40, but a claim that three quarters of pregnancies miscarry at ages 35 to 39 is not a sound general estimate. Both being underweight and being overweight can be associated with increased risk. These are population patterns, not an explanation of why an individual loss happened.

Stopping smoking, discussing a sustainable healthy weight and eating a varied diet with fruit and vegetables are sensible preparation steps. They cannot guarantee that miscarriage will be prevented. Seek help with any ongoing health condition and ask about the usual preconception checks and supplements for your circumstances.

Ordinary stress is not established as a cause of miscarriage. Rest, counseling or practical support can help you cope, but being less anxious is not a treatment you must achieve to deserve a healthy pregnancy. The loss was not a failure of effort.

Emotional readiness may follow its own timetable

You and a partner may feel ready at different times. Talk about what trying again would mean, whether tracking helps or overwhelms you, and what support you would want during another pregnancy. Friends, family, a pregnancy-loss support service or a clinician can help without setting a deadline.

You can ask for a plan for the next positive test while also deciding to wait. If grief, anxiety or low mood is making daily life difficult, ask for professional support. Returning ovulation is a biological change, not an instruction to move on.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Fertility can return before the first period. The earliest possible ovulation date is not a reliable forecast for an individual cycle.

Research does not support imposing the same six-month delay after every uncomplicated early miscarriage. Recovery and any specific treatment determine personal advice.

How BeMama can help

At follow-up, ask what marks completion of your recovery, when a pregnancy test should become negative, and whether your history changes the plan for trying again.

When to seek help

Seek urgent help for heavy bleeding with weakness or faintness, severe pain or feeling very unwell. Contact your care team promptly about fever, offensive discharge or symptoms that are not settling.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Ovulation can precede the first period after a miscarriage.
  • Record recovery bleeding separately from a normal cycle.
  • Waiting advice should fit the loss and recovery, not an automatic six-month rule.
  • LH tests and temperature patterns have limitations after pregnancy.
  • Ask for earlier fertility or recurrent-loss advice when your history warrants it.
  • Physical and emotional readiness do not have to happen together.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get pregnant before my first period after miscarriage?

Yes. Ovulation occurs before a period and can return quickly. Use contraception if you do not want another pregnancy yet.

Is two weeks the usual ovulation date for everyone?

No. It is an early possibility after an early loss, not a prediction. Hormone levels and recovery vary.

When will my periods be regular again?

The first period often returns within several weeks, but a predictable pattern can take longer. Previous irregularity may continue; discuss prolonged absence of periods or unresolved symptoms with your care team.

Must I wait for six months or one period?

Neither is a universal rule after an uncomplicated early miscarriage. One period can help date the next pregnancy. Complete follow-up and ask whether your treatment or recovery requires a delay.

Can an ovulation strip prove that fertility has returned?

No. It detects a hormone pattern, not an egg. Recent pregnancy can affect some products, so follow the specific instructions and seek advice if results are confusing.

Does a temperature rise identify the best day to try?

It usually reflects a change after ovulation. The fertile days generally come before that sustained rise, so temperature alone has limited predictive value.

When should I get help if I have not conceived?

Usual assessment thresholds are 12 months under age 35 and six months from age 35, with earlier discussion over 40 or when there are known problems. Include the time you were trying before the miscarriage.

Does repeat miscarriage mean there must be a genetic problem?

No. An assessment may consider several possible causes, and it sometimes finds none. Discuss repeated losses with a clinician rather than choosing tests on your own.

Could ordinary stress have caused my miscarriage?

It is not an established cause. Support for distress is valuable for your wellbeing; the loss should not be blamed on your emotions.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
